title: Statistical Power and Type M Error
summary: Set an effect you assume is real and watch alpha, beta and power become three areas that move together. Then run two thousand simulated studies and compare every estimate with only the significant ones.
learningObjectives: Identify alpha, beta and power as areas on two sampling distributions.
Work out the sample size a planned study needs for a stated effect and target power.
Explain why observed power computed after a study adds nothing to its p-value.
Explain how conditioning on significance exaggerates effects without biasing any individual study.
Recognise Type S errors, where a significant result points the wrong way.
topics: Type I and Type II error
interactionTypes: two live sampling distributions with shaded error regions
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every study is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radio groups, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the Type M sample-size slider announces both the size and the power it produces. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired inside their figures with visible tables - power, beta, alpha and the rejection threshold for the first, and a seven-row summary including the exaggeration ratio and the count of wrong-signed significant results for the second - and a disclosure holds the sample size required at each of four target power levels. The alpha and beta regions are hatched in opposite directions as well as differently tinted, the null curve is dashed and the alternative solid, both are labelled inside the picture, and the three reference lines on the Type M histogram differ in dash pattern and carry printed labels, so nothing depends on colour. Pinned primary results measure 514px and 565px tall at 1366x768. Every control, preset and run announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to each experiment's heading as it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Power as four areas, the sample size a study would need, and why significant small studies exaggerate
simulationNotes: In Experiment 1 the observed effect size is treated as approximately normal with standard error the square root of two over n. The rejection threshold uses the exact critical value of t on 2n-2 degrees of freedom converted to the d scale, and the area beyond it is computed from a normal rather than a non-central t; at these sample sizes the difference is a fraction of a percentage point, the page says so in its limitations, and the required sample sizes it produces match published tables - 64 per group for 80% power at d = 0.50 and 253 at d = 0.25, both at alpha .05. Required n is found by scanning upwards until the target is reached. Experiment 2 does not approximate: it generates two thousand real experiments, each drawing two groups of n from Normal(0,1) and Normal(0.35,1), computing the pooled standard deviation, the observed d and the t statistic, and declaring significance when the statistic reaches the exact critical value. At fifteen per group and seed 5477 this gives 301 significant results out of 2000, a mean estimate across all studies of 0.35 - unbiased - a mean among the significant ones of 0.97, an exaggeration ratio of 2.76, and three significant results with the wrong sign; at a hundred and twenty per group the ratio falls to 1.17 and no sign errors remain. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. No real study, participant or literature is involved.
